title: Logic and conditions
detect: ตารางความจริง
grading_guide: Check every branch of the student's conditions, including exact boundary values (e.g. 600 and 601 when ranges are 1-600 / 601-1800).
Different but equivalent conditions are correct: reversed order (largest range first), x > 600 instead of x >= 601 for integers, separate if statements with && ranges, or switch(true).
Deduct for a boundary only when a concrete input actually lands in the wrong branch.
Conditions in an else-if chain are evaluated in order; later conditions only see inputs that failed earlier ones, so they may be written shorter.

concepts.text: Operator precedence: ! binds tightest, then &&, then ||. a || b && c means a || (b && c). Comparison operators (<, ===) bind tighter than && and ||.
&& stops at the first falsy operand and returns it; || stops at the first truthy operand and returns it. ?? returns the right side only when the left is null or undefined.
De Morgan: !(a && b) equals !a || !b, and !(a || b) equals !a && !b. false && anything is false; true || anything is true.
JavaScript does not support math-style chains: 1 < x < 10 is evaluated as (1 < x) < 10, which is always true because the boolean becomes 0 or 1. A correct range check is x > 1 && x < 10.
Ranges like '1-600' and '601-1800' are inclusive. For integer inputs, x <= 600 equals x < 601 and x > 600 equals x >= 601. Using < 600 instead of <= 600 misplaces exactly x = 600.

In if / else if / else only the first true branch runs. Separate if statements can run several branches, which is only correct when the conditions are mutually exclusive. A dangling else belongs to the nearest unmatched if.
n % 2 === 0 tests even. For negative odd numbers n % 2 is -1, so n % 2 === 1 misses them; n % 2 !== 0 tests odd for all integers.
cond ? a : b is an expression equal to a when cond is truthy, otherwise b. Nested ternaries are equivalent to an else-if chain.
